text:
Research Mentoring & Lab Service
Undergraduate Research Mentor (2023 – present) Cognitive Neuroscience of Perception, Attention, and Memory Lab, University of California, Riverside

Train undergraduate research assistants in experimental procedures, participant testing, and data collection for studies of visual working memory and mnemonic discrimination.
Guide data analysis and computational modeling, including MATLAB code, mixture-model fitting, visualization, and interpretation of behavioral results.
Mentor undergraduate teams in abstract writing, poster design, and presentation preparation for UCLA’s Psychology Undergraduate Research Conference, UCR’s Undergraduate Research & Creative Activities Symposium, and R’PSYC (2025–2026).
Provide ongoing manuscript guidance to Kara Nguyen and Daniel Punzalan on working memory and mnemonic discrimination, including feedback on analyses, figures, scientific writing, and revisions for an undergraduate research journal submission.
Coordinate research-assistant meetings, journal-club discussions, and onboarding and training with senior undergraduate researchers; support students in developing independent research and scientific communication skills.

I am a Ph.D. student in the Department of Psychology at the University of California, Riverside, working in the Cognitive Neuroscience of Perception, Attention, and Memory Lab under the supervision of Dr. Weiwei Zhang.
My research broadly focuses on visual representations using psychophysics, computational modeling, and ERP.
Before joining UCR, I completed my B.A. and M.A. in Psychology at Jeonbuk National University (South Korea) , where I studied affective neuroscience and psychophysics with Dr. Jongwan Kim and Dr. Chang-Ho Park.




what determines the quality (precision) of a remembered representation? Select a figure to enlarge it.



Kim, Won, Acebo, & Zhang · VSS 2025 conference poster
Distinguishing similar objects in long-term memory (LTM) can interfere with the precision of short-term memory (STM). In a dual-task experiment, a high demand on lure discrimination reduced the precision of STM for orientations, while it had a little impact on the memory probability of STM. These behavioral findings support the idea of representational competition between STM precision and LTM lure discrimination.



ROC mixture-model estimates in Experiment 2 (n = 44). Precision (d′) was reduced during MST lure trials relative to target and foil trials; memory-success probability (Pm, labeled capacity) showed no detected difference.


View VSS 2025 poster



Kim, Ma, Liu, & Zhang · VSS 2026 conference poster
Does a less accurate memory reflect a weaker signal or a less precise representation? Using a random-dot motion (RDM) recall task and a modified Target Confusability Competition model (Schurgin, M. W., Wixted, J. T., & Brady, T. F. 2020), we estimated memory strength (d′) and precision (κ) separately.
Motion variability: Increasing directional noise from low to moderate levels reduced precision with little change in strength. At the highest noise level, both estimates worsened.



Experiment 1 (n = 38): parameter estimates across motion-variability conditions and model comparisons. Between low and moderate noise, the model allowing precision to vary while fixing strength was preferred for 23 of 38 participants.


Motion coherence: Higher coherence increased strength but decreased the estimated precision. Model comparisons favored a strength-varying, fixed-precision model for 27 of 36 participants. The pattern supports distinct effects of the two noise manipulations, while also showing a trade-off between the fitted parameters.



Experiment 2 (n = 36): precision and strength estimates for low (80%) and high (100%) coherence, alongside model comparisons. Higher coherence increased strength and reduced the estimated precision.
